message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

The case for a weekend rate rise is plausible: you are priced below the competitive set and sold out 31 Saturdays. But the proposal has a factual inconsistency that inflates the headline figure, weak evidence on price sensitivity, and a two-night minimum that conflicts with the hotel's own booking data. It shouldn't be approved as written.

## Major issues

**1. The room count is inconsistent, and the wrong figure drives the revenue estimate.**
Section 2 says Harbourside has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124 rooms**.
- With 124 rooms: 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£204,000**
- With 112 rooms: 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**

If 112 is correct, the headline is overstated by about £20,000 (around 10%). This needs confirming before anything else.

**2. The price-sensitivity evidence is confounded by seasonality.**
Section 3 attributes the June-to-July 2025 rise (81% → 89%) to the £10 rate increase. Section 2 already explains that rise: July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. A seasonal peak following a late-June price change says almost nothing about price sensitivity. The claim that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning" has no support in the data.

Better evidence would include:
- July–September 2025 compared with the same months in 2024, when the rate was unchanged
- Pace and pick-up for comparable weekends booked before and after the change
- Competitor rate movements over the same period

**3. "Maintained occupancy" is the optimistic case, not the prudent one.**
Assuming no occupancy loss after a 14% price rise is the best-case scenario. The recommendation then calls the result a floor ("at least £204,000"), which is not justified. The proposal should include a sensitivity range. A useful reference point: at £165, weekend room revenue breaks even at about **69% occupancy** (79% × 145/165). So occupancy could fall by roughly 9–10 points before the rise loses money. That is a reasonably strong argument for the proposal, and it is more credible than claiming no loss at all.

**4. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business.**
Section 4 states that weddings at Quayside Hall account for about **38% of Saturday-night bookings**, and that these guests stay one night, Saturday to Sunday. A two-night minimum would apply directly to that segment. The likely outcomes are lost wedding blocks to competitors, or a blanket exemption that removes much of the policy's effect. Only already-contracted group business is protected (Section 6), so future wedding blocks are exposed. Either exempt wedding and group blocks explicitly and re-estimate the policy's effect, or reconsider the minimum.

More generally, the assumption that single-night Saturday guests will "convert" to two nights is untested. Some will book elsewhere. On the 31 sell-out Saturdays you are already full, so a minimum could displace higher-value Saturday-only demand rather than add Friday or Sunday nights.

**5. The £20 increase is applied to every occupied room, not just BAR business.**
The calculation multiplies all occupied weekend rooms by £20. Only rooms sold at BAR (or rates linked to it) will see the increase. Corporate contracted rates, group and wedding blocks, packages and some OTA rates won't. With 38% of Saturdays in wedding blocks alone, the real uplift is materially lower. OTA commission on the increase also reduces net gain.

## Moderate issues

- **The first-year figure ignores bookings already on the books.** Rates load on 15 May for stays from 1 June, so much of June–August, your peak period, will already be sold at £145. Year-one gain will fall well short of the annual run-rate.
- **The 2025 baseline mixes two rate levels.** The weekend rate was £135 until late June 2025 and £145 afterwards, so the 79% average isn't a clean baseline at £145.
- **The value-for-money score was measured at the old price.** A score of 8.4 at £135–£145 doesn't predict perception at £165. It's also unclear how competitors' scores were obtained.
- **The competitor comparison is rate-only.** It doesn't establish that Harbourside is comparable on product, location or reviews to hotels charging £165–£180. Moving to £165 puts you at the bottom of their range, which is defensible, but say so.
- **Fridays and Saturdays are treated together.** Saturday demand is clearly constrained. Friday may not be. A differentiated approach (e.g. a larger Saturday increase and a smaller Friday one) may capture more revenue with less risk.

## Minor issues

- The "recovered strongly since 2023" claim has no supporting data. Add 2023–2024 figures or remove it.
- Two weeks' notice to OTAs may be shorter than some contracts require. Worth checking.
- The monitoring trigger tracks occupancy only. Given the break-even point above, **weekend RevPAR** against 2025 is the better measure, alongside occupancy.
- Introducing the price rise and the minimum stay together makes it hard to tell which caused any change. Consider phasing them or testing the minimum on selected weekends first.

## Note on timing

The document is dated April 2026 for a 1 June start. If it was implemented, about five months of actual results are now available. Comparing June–October 2026 against 2025 (occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, length of stay and wedding-block volume) would be far stronger evidence than anything in the current draft.

## Suggested revisions

1. Confirm the room count and recalculate.
2. Restrict the uplift to BAR-linked business and net off OTA commission.
3. Replace the June/July comparison with a year-on-year or pace-based analysis.
4. Add a sensitivity table (e.g. occupancy flat, −3, −5, −10 points) and show the ~69% break-even.
5. Exempt wedding and group blocks from the two-night minimum, or drop it, and estimate its effect explicitly.
6. Show a separate first-year figure that accounts for business already booked.
7. Monitor RevPAR, not just occupancy.
